query: Reported superconducting high-entropy alloys are dominated by Nb-Ta matrices, while other studies concern titanium-rich systems based on heavy transition metals and partly ordered systems. Consequently, these precedents do not establish what controls superconductivity in high-entropy alloys outside the best-studied material classes. Within the defining constraint of a solid solution containing at least five elements at no less than 5 atomic percent each, what governs superconducting behavior in such an uncharacterized high-entropy alloy, and why? State one testable mechanistic hypothesis, a controlled comparison against the starting material, predicted observations relative to the baseline, applicable boundary conditions, the earlier evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In uncharacterized high‐entropy alloys, modest, controlled compositional tuning that reduces local lattice distortion enhances electron–phonon coupling and thereby increases the superconducting transition temperature (Tc) relative to a baseline equiatomic solid solution.
generation.material_initial_state: A disordered, single‐phase equiatomic high‐entropy alloy (at least five elements present at no less than 5 atomic percent each) with a baseline Tc measured under low-temperature conditions.
generation.intervention: Perform a controlled compositional tuning experiment by gradually substituting one of the constituent elements with an isoelectronic element known to reduce lattice strain, while maintaining a single-phase, equiatomic solid solution.
generation.conditions: Low-temperature measurements (e.g., 2–10 K) under conditions ensuring phase stability (no phase separation or ordering) and using identical processing routes for all samples.
generation.structural_mediator: Modulated lattice distortion and local bonding environment.
generation.mechanism: Reduction in local lattice distortion decreases scattering and enhances electron–phonon coupling, which in turn raises the superconducting Tc. Conversely, increases in lattice distortion would be expected to lower Tc.
generation.predicted_outcome: The controlled substitution that lessens lattice distortion will result in a systematic increase in Tc compared to the baseline HEA. In contrast, if the substitution inadvertently increases lattice disorder, a decrease in Tc is expected.
generation.baseline: The superconducting transition temperature (Tc) as measured in the starting equiatomic high-entropy alloy without compositional modifications.
generation.boundary: This effect is expected to be observable only in single-phase, disordered solid solutions. If the composition change leads to phase separation or the formation of ordered structures, the mechanism may not hold.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the Tc shift is uncertain due to potential interplay of electronic structure effects and may vary with the specific choice of substituent element.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of HEA samples based on the same equiatomic baseline and systematically substitute a fixed fraction of one element with an isoelectronic substitute known to influence lattice distortion. Characterize the phase purity via X-ray diffraction and measure the Tc using electrical resistivity and magnetic susceptibility under identical low-temperature conditions.
measurements: Superconducting transition temperature (Tc) via resistivity drop and magnetic susceptibility (Meissner effect)
Lattice parameters and strain via high-resolution XRD
Microstructural uniformity (e.g., by SEM or TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the variations in Tc across the substitution series do not correlate with the measured changes in lattice distortion (i.e., if reducing distortion does not lead to a systematic increase in Tc, or if Tc changes unpredictably contrary to the mechanistic prediction), then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In 2014, the first superconducting high-entropy alloy Ta0.34Nb0.33Hf0.08Zr0.14Ti0.11 (in at.%) was discovered []. According to Sun and Cava [], this alloy can be classified as a type-A HEA superconductor. HEAs of this type contain only metals on the left side of the transition metal region of the periodic table, crystallize in a body-centered cubic (bcc) lattice, and exhibit superconducting transition temperatures (Tc) between 4.0 and 9.2 K, while their highest upper critical field (μ0Hc2) is close to 12 T [,,,,,,]. These are the most widely studied HEA superconductors to date. However, it should be noted that most of these alloys contain a large amount of niobium and tantalum, while the titanium concentration is typically less than 20 at.%. Because binary Nb-Ti alloys exhibit much better superconducting properties than Nb-Ta [], it is plausible to expect that NbTi-based high-entropy alloys will have a higher Tc and/or μ0Hc2 compared to previously reported type-A HEA superconductors. Moreover, in the case of various ternary Nb-Ti-Hf and Nb-Ti-Ta and quaternary Nb-Ti-Ta-Hf alloys, the highest values of μ0Hc2 were observed for the titanium-rich alloys []. frame.system: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) that form a solid solution with at least five elements present at no less than 5 atomic percent each. The starting state includes systems previously dominated by Nb–Ta matrices or titanium‐rich heavy transition metal compositions, with limited characterization beyond these established classes.
frame.goal: To elucidate and control the mechanism governing superconductivity in uncharacterized high-entropy alloys, thereby providing a general understanding beyond the narrow classes studied so far.
frame.limitation: Existing studies are limited to Nb–Ta based and titanium-rich systems (including partly ordered structures), leaving the controlling factors behind superconducting behavior in the broader compositional space of HEAs unclear.
root_cause_cues: Reported superconducting high-entropy alloys are dominated by Nb-Ta matrices
other studies concern titanium-rich systems based on heavy transition metals
do not establish what controls superconductivity in high-entropy alloys
constraints: each element present at no less than 5 atomic percent
frame.regime: Low-temperature conditions required for superconductivity measurements (e.g., measurements of Tc under cryogenic conditions) while maintaining the phase stability of a multi-element solid solution.
prior_attempts: Studies targeting Nb–Ta matrices which successfully demonstrated superconductivity but did not reveal universal governing principles for HEAs.
Investigations on titanium-rich systems that tentatively linked chemical composition to superconducting properties but lacked sufficient breadth to generalize across the HEA compositional space.

families.principle: Utilizing systematic compositional variations to isolate the effect of individual elemental concentrations on superconducting behavior, thereby directly linking macroscopic experimental controls to variations in Tc and other superconducting properties.

families.best_lever: Perform controlled compositional tuning experiments (e.g., gradual substitution of one element while maintaining the overall five-element solid solution) and directly measure changes in superconducting transition temperature.
